I have not noticed a building of resistance, that is to say, my general mental state hasn't deteriorated to pre-medicated levels in any noticeable degree. Rather, I am more productive and motivated and ambitious than I ever thought I could be pre-medication. If there is a resistance being built, it's gradual to the extreme. The thing is, even if that were the case, and such a resistance did occur, my understanding of how these drugs work is that it wouldn't bring about the opposite of its intended effect.

Certain drug interactions, on the other hand, can cause a an inverse or reverse of the intended effect - such as re-uptake inhibitors mixed with alcohol. I don't drink alcohol anymore, and it's largely because I'm on medication. A lot of medicated individuals - such as my bi-polar aunt, will choose to skip a dose because she plans to drink alcohol that day. But that's not how it works. The substance is still in your system, even if you skip a day. So the interaction is still very likely.

Another major concern is simply stopping treatment. In that case, there can be and often is a 'slingshot' effect, where a sudden mood swing in precisely the wrong direction happens. And some people will do this, for the same reason some people stop taking anti-biotics as soon as they start to feel better.

If a person is being treated with psychotropic medication, and either chooses to imbibe alcohol during treatment, or simply stop treatment, there can be some severe, and quite possibly suicidal or homicidal side effects. But I would not place blame on the substance itself for those effects. Just as I would not blame the weapon itself for any resultant homicides or suicides.

But what you say is still accurate: the potency of these drugs is tremendous, and can be extremely dangerous. I lived with persistent depression for my entire adolescence and the first half of my 20s. It's not what a healthy mind conjures when he thinks of depression. I resisted multiple attempts to get my to start medication, going back to age 16, precisely because I believed that the unambitious youth of profoundly dismal and morbid demeanor was "just who I was". My biggest ambition was to be like Edgar Allen Poe.

For most, the idea of depression is inherently temporary, and has more to do with external factors than anything. But for someone in my situation, depression means an intrinsic malaise that just plain doesn't go away. It has nothing to do with weather, what people say, whether you've eaten or showered that day, how much you slept, etc. Speaking of sleep, if I was idle, that is, my mind wasn't occupied, I was sleepy. And if I did fall asleep, it wasn't the least bit restful - in fact, sleep itself wasn't restful.

People will often talk about how physical exercise helped them out of depression. And that's good for them. I can't remember who said it, but "what a shame it is for a man to die without knowing the great feats of which his body is capable," or something along those lines. And exercise is always a first resort for dealing with depression. But there are those for whom that doesn't address the core cause. I was in the Army for 3 years before I started my prescription. I was active every day. I competed in and completed Iron Man competitions, a few times in the top 5. It didn't help. On the way back to the barracks after work, I had to make sure I stopped at the mess hall before I got home, because if I went home, I wasn't going anywhere else. Didn't matter how hungry I was, I just didn't have the energy.

For a healthy person, or a person who is depressed in reaction to an external factor, the depression is ultimately temporary, and there is an intrinsic understanding of this. But for a person with chronic depression, any feelings of heightened energy or satisfaction are always quite temporary, and thus feel entirely artificial. Even sex felt more like a chemical high than anything else. I know what chemical highs feel like because I tiptoed around that path, too.

Moral of the textwall: don't put a moratorium on these drugs, as there are those that need them. But put an age limit on their prescription, at the very least. Prior to that, other measures should be pursued to see of the still developing brain can be coaxed back into healthy function the old fashioned ways - activity, competition, healthy socializing, etc.
